# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Review: "Two Years On", the Varden 24-month follow-up and Halden subset

**Bottom line:** this is the most informative paper in the set. It meets the standards the critics asked for: a randomised comparison, record-based output, a second, stricter hours measure, a two-year follow-up, and a mediation test registered before outcomes were known. It also checks the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies and finds the problem my previous review suspected. The main conclusions hold up: the per-hour gain is smaller than at nine months but has not disappeared, and the counter arm failed.

The paper misses one important point. **The control group was contaminated after the nine-month results were published**, and that alone could explain roughly half of the apparent decline. There are also problems with how the decline is summarised, with the strength of the mediation claim, and with a few figures that don't reconcile.

## What checks out

| Check | Calculation | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Output per hour, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% ✓ |
| Halden, 11 continuing organisations | 0.968 / (34.9/40.3 = 0.866) = 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Counter staffing needed | 1 / 0.886 (output per FTE at 9 months) = 1.129 | "12% more staff" ✓ (approximately) |

Section 5's point about the meta-analysis is the most important correction to the literature. The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so the meta-analysis's claim of "no sign of decay" falls apart.

---

## 1. The control offices were contaminated, which biases the decline upward

In month 15, two control offices carried out a meeting audit and cut their meetings. The paper treats this as a side observation. In fact it is contamination of the comparison group, and it most likely came from the trial itself. The nine-month report, which highlighted meetings, had been published months earlier.

**Rough size of the effect:**
- The two offices raised their output per hour by about 4.1%.
- Spread across all seven control offices, that lifts the control average by about 2/7 × 4.1 ≈ **1.2 points**.
- The like-for-like decline in the measured gain is **2.7 points** (12.5% → 9.8%).
- So **roughly half the apparent fading** could be the control offices improving, not the treated offices declining.

This cuts both ways for the paper's conclusions:
- The fading reported in Section 3 may be overstated.
- The 24-month gain may be *understated* as an estimate of the effect against an uncontaminated control.

**Fix:**
- Report the 24-month estimates with those two offices excluded, and alternatively censored from month 15.
- Report the treated and control output-per-hour trends separately, so readers can see which side moved.
- Name this explicitly as a limitation.

**A useful cross-check.** The meetings pathway accounts for about 47% of an 8.5% gain, roughly 4 points. The audit offices gained 4.1% from a smaller cut in meetings and with no change in hours. That is weak, uncontrolled evidence, but it fits the paper's suggestion that some of the gain might be available through reorganisation alone.

## 2. The summary compares figures measured differently

- **The Summary mixes two hours measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% uses timesheets and the 8.5% uses system logs. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**. The extra 1.3 points come from the stricter measure, not from the passage of time. Section 3 gets this right, so the Summary should match it.
- **"Declined by about a quarter"** (Section 5) is a fifth on the like-for-like measure (2.7 / 12.5 = 22%), before any adjustment for contamination.
- **The decline isn't statistically established.** The nine-month and 24-month intervals overlap almost entirely (6.9–18.4 vs 4.6–15.2). Estimate the change directly, within offices, with its own interval. If it doesn't exclude zero, say "consistent with some fading" (as Section 3 already does), not "has declined".
- **Two time points can't show a trajectory.** This is the same objection I raised against the Halden re-analysis's two-point extrapolation of energy scores. Timesheet output per hour should exist for every month, so report the monthly path. A gain that levels off near 10% and one still falling steadily have very different implications.

## 3. The mediation result is promising but "confirms" is too strong

- **Clustering.** The intervals (28–66% and 2–34%) look narrow for a study with 7 treated and 7 control offices. "A larger sample of office-months" is not the right basis for inference, because months within an office are not independent. State how the standard errors were clustered, and consider randomisation inference for the indirect effects.
- **Mediators weren't randomised.** The Limitations section rightly notes the no-confounding assumption. The most obvious confounder is manager quality: managers who cut meetings may also improve workflow in other ways. Meeting reductions would then pick up credit for the whole bundle.
- **The two mediators aren't independent.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. Unless the model allowed for this, the 47 / 18 split depends on modelling assumptions. Report which decomposition was used.
- **This is a confirmatory test in the same offices, not a replication.** The hypothesis came from these seven treated offices and the registered test was run on the same seven. Pre-registration protects against flexible analysis, not against features peculiar to these offices. "Survives a registered test" is fair; "confirms" (Summary) is too strong.
- **Where did the baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This paper reports baseline figures (7.4 vs 7.2). If these were retrieved retrospectively from calendar systems, say so. They are reassuring: groups that look balanced at baseline answer the concern I raised about pre-existing differences.

## 4. Figures that need reconciling

**Control-office meeting time.**
- Control offices averaged 7.0 hours per week at month 24.
- The two audit offices fell to 5.0, presumably still lower at month 24.
- The other five offices must therefore average about (49 − 10) / 5 ≈ **7.8 hours**, *up* from a baseline of about 7.2.
- Either the audit offices drifted back, or meeting time in other control offices rose. Either way, report it.

**What the system logs include.**
- "Active log-in time on the case-management system" presumably excludes meetings.
- If so, treated offices would show a much smaller fall on logs than on timesheets, because they cut about 3.5 hours of meetings and some of that time would have moved to logged casework.
- Yet the two measures fall almost equally (−11% vs −12%).
- Either logs count time logged in during meetings, in which case "active" is overstated, or something else accounts for the similarity. Define the measure precisely.

This also matters for the mediation result. If meetings are excluded from logged hours, cutting them cannot raise output per *logged* hour simply by freeing time. It would have to work through better focus during case hours. That is a narrower mechanism than "removing low-value time", and the interpretation should match it.

## 5. The Halden subset

- **The baseline figure needs checking.** The baseline hours figure, 40.3, is exactly the average of Varga & Holm's 27 time-tracking organisations. Is it the baseline for *these 11* organisations? If it was carried over from the larger group, the 11.8% is not a within-organisation calculation.
- **Do all 11 have time tracking?** Only 17 of the original 23 had both records and time tracking. Say how many of the 11 do.
- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations contacted did not provide data. Non-responders may include more reverted or struggling organisations. The authors already call these figures an upper bound, which is appropriate, but the non-response should be quantified.
- **One reversion came from discretionary work.** A marketing agency reverted, citing client deadlines. That is not coverage-bound work in the meta-analysis's sense, so the Summary's "client-facing or coverage obligations" may blur a real point. Deadline-driven client work can behave like coverage-bound work. That supports the meta-analysis's caution about forcing work into binary categories.
- **"Upper bound" holds only for selection.** With no comparison group across 2.5 years, trends in the wider economy and the sector could bias the estimate in either direction.
- **Conflict of interest.** One co-author also wrote the original Halden paper. That's not a problem in itself, but a statement of interests is normal practice.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Ending the counter arm.** The county ended the counter arm at month 12, which deviates from the original plan. Report this as a protocol deviation. The month 10–12 waiting-time comparison against control (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes) is a useful improvement on the nine-month report's treated-only before-and-after figures.
- **The staffing figure covers throughput, not waiting times.** The 12% staffing estimate restores the *number of contacts handled*. In queueing work, bringing waits back to baseline may need more than that, because part of the per-hour gain came from higher utilisation. The 9% cost estimate is therefore probably a lower bound.
- **Secondary outcomes are still reported as levels.** Appeal overturns and resignations are given as levels rather than difference-in-differences with intervals, as in the nine-month report. At 24 months there are enough appeals and resignations to estimate both properly.
- **Output per worker.** The per-FTE interval (−8.0 to +1.2) still allows a meaningful loss. "Mostly, not fully, offset" is a fair description.

---

## Where the five papers now leave the question

| Question | Best current answer | Change from previous synthesis |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | ~8.5–10% at 24 months in the one randomised study; possibly higher against an uncontaminated control | Narrowed; strongest evidence now comes from a two-year randomised comparison |
| Durability | Modest fading from 9 to 24 months, possibly half of it due to control contamination; not zero | Partly answered; still needs the monthly trajectory |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported | Settled |
| "No sign of decay" (meta-analysis) | Not supported; it rested on four uncontrolled scheduled-hours studies | Settled |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings is the largest measured pathway; fatigue smaller; about a third unexplained | New, but from a same-sample test; needs replication elsewhere |
| Reorganisation without cutting hours | Suggestive evidence from two contaminated control offices | Open, and now the key policy question |
| Coverage-bound work | Fails on service quality and cost; arm ended | Settled for this setting |

The best next study is the one this paper identifies but couldn't run: a **three-arm trial** comparing reduced hours, reorganisation (meeting audit and workflow changes) at standard hours, and an unchanged control. It would need safeguards against control offices adopting the intervention, such as delaying publication of interim results.
